Install of compromised @asyncapi npm package versions (generator/helpers/components/specs) AIDelivery High
Hunts for developer or CI hosts installing the specific poisoned @asyncapi package versions published on 2026-07-14 that carry the Miasma dropper. Grounded on the exact package@version strings from the article, so it flags exposure regardless of whether the module was ever require()d. Rationale: Uses the five exact compromised package@version strings named in the article and confirmed by Socket/StepSecurity/OX Security. These versions were unpublished, so any residual reference is high-fidelity exposure evidence. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A remediation/IR engineer intentionally installing the pinned bad version in an isolated lab to reverse it
  • An internal mirror serving a cached copy that still lists the old version in a lockfile audit command
  • Security scanner (e.g. Socket/Snyk CLI) echoing the package@version string in its own command line while auditing
  • A developer typing the version in a `npm view @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1` diagnostic command
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "npm view" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "audit"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which host/user ran the install and whether it was a build/CI agent or a dev laptop; check DeviceProcessEvents for any node.exe child spawned shortly after. 2) Contain: isolate the host, rotate any credentials reachable from it (npm tokens, GitHub CLI, AWS keys, SSH keys, browser sessions) and remove the package from the affected lockfile/registry cache. 3) Hunt: pivot to IPFS gateway fetches of CID QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9, sync.js file drops, and outbound connections to 85.137.53.71.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm") or ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","node","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("@asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1","@asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1","@asyncapi/generator@3.3.1","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2","@asyncapi/specs@6.11.2-alpha.1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName

Node.js spawns detached background node fetching Miasma stage-2 from IPFS gatewa AIDelivery High
Hunts the require()-time dropper behaviour where a node/npm process launches a detached child node that pulls the encrypted stage-2 (sync.js) from the IPFS gateway. Anchored on the article's IPFS CID and gateway path rather than a generic node-spawns-node pattern. Rationale: Combines the article's parent-child chain (module load -> detached node) with the exact IPFS CID/gateway path and sync.js loader name, giving a high-fidelity delivery-stage detection distinct from generic node execution. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legit IPFS-based dev tool (e.g. js-ipfs/Helia) fetching content via ipfs.io through node
  • A frontend project genuinely named sync.js being launched with node during a build
  • A developer manually curl-ing an IPFS gateway inside an npm run script for testing
  • Package tarball integrity tooling referencing an ipfs.io mirror
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9" or ProcessCommandLine has "sync.js"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full child node command line and the parent lockfile/module path; confirm the CID matches QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9. 2) Contain: kill the detached node process tree, isolate the host, and block the IPFS gateway CID at proxy. 3) Hunt: look for sync.js written to temp/appdata, registry Run-key persistence written by node, and beacons to 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091.
DeviceProcessEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FileName =~ "node.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs.io/ipfs/","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","sync.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm")
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs.io/ipfs/","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","sync.js")

IPFS gateway fetch of Miasma stage-2 CID (ipfs.io/ipfs/QmQobZSp...) AIDelivery High
Network-layer detection for a host retrieving the encrypted second stage from the exact IPFS CID hosted on ipfs.io. Pivots on the CID string in the URL, which uniquely identifies this campaign's payload regardless of the fetching process. Rationale: The IPFS CID QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9 in the download URL is a unique campaign IOC confirmed across Socket, SafeDep and Datadog; the URL-path match is near-zero FP. DNS-only fallback (ipfs.io + node) is used where proxy telemetry is absent. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of the public ipfs.io gateway by a decentralized-app developer
  • A CI job resolving ipfs.io for an unrelated, benign CID (only the DNS fallback clause, not the CID clause)
  • Security researcher fetching the CID for analysis from a sanctioned host
  • Corporate proxy prefetch/cache warming ipfs.io
Suppression filter
DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemoteUrl has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the URL contained the exact CID (true positive) vs a generic ipfs.io hit (needs enrichment); identify the fetching process. 2) Contain: block the CID/gateway at web proxy and isolate the host if the CID matched. 3) Hunt: correlate to the node parent chain, sync.js drop, persistence writes, and 85.137.53.71 beaconing on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9"
   or (RemoteUrl has "ipfs.io" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9" or Url has "ipfs.io/ipfs"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma sync.js loader dropped to OS-specific path by node and executed AIInstallation Medium
Detects the encrypted stage-2 JavaScript loader 'sync.js' being written by a node/npm process to a staging path, the precursor to Miasma tasking-framework execution. Scoped to node-parented writes plus temp/appdata/hidden-dir staging seen in the campaign. Rationale: sync.js is the article's named stage-2 loader; pairing the exact filename with a node/npm writer and the campaign's staging locations (temp/appdata/.config/.cache/node_modules per Datadog & CybersecurityNews) keeps FPs on the common filename manageable. Cross-checked against: • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-turns-trusted-npm-packages-into-persistent-backdoors/ • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browsersync/webpack-dev-server writing a sync.js helper during a build
  • A project that legitimately ships a module named sync.js into node_modules
  • Editor autosave dropping sync.js into an AppData temp workspace
  • Test frameworks generating sync.js fixtures in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.config/.miasma", "mesa_shader_cache") or SHA256 in ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1","082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab","bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped sync.js and compare to the article SHA256 set; inspect the writing node command line and parent package. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and rotate developer credentials if execution followed the write. 3) Hunt: check for immediate outbound to ipfs.io CID or 85.137.53.71, plus systemd/launchd/Run-key persistence created by the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\node_modules\", @"\ProgramData\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", "/.config/", "/.cache/", "/tmp/", "node_modules")

Miasma botnet C2 beacon to 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound connections from any endpoint to the confirmed Miasma C2 host 85.137.53.71 (AS43641, NL) — command server 8080, exfil 8081, proxy-mgmt 8091. IP-anchored so it fires regardless of which of the six C2 channels is used. Rationale: 85.137.53.71 is the confirmed Miasma C2 IP (StepSecurity/Rescana attribute 8080 command, 8081 exfil, 8091 proxy-mgmt on AS43641). A hard IP match with per-port summarization is a low-FP, high-severity C2 detection. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-alert-asyncapi-npm-supply-chain-attack-delivers-multi-stage-miasma-botnet-via-compromised-github-act
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel/IR analyst deliberately connecting to the C2 from a sanctioned sandbox for analysis
  • A shared-hosting IP reassignment where 85.137.53.71 later serves benign content (validate timestamp against disclosure date)
  • Internet-wide scanner infrastructure your org runs hitting the same IP
  • A VPN/proxy egress node coincidentally sharing the subnet (verify exact /32)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and destination port (8080/8081/8091 map to command/exfil/proxy) and whether the host imported an @asyncapi package. 2) Contain: block 85.137.53.71 at the firewall/proxy, isolate the host, and treat as data-theft (rotate npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH creds and wallets). 3) Hunt: expand to the full IOC set — IPFS CID fetch, sync.js drop, systemd miasma-monitor.service / Run-key persistence — across all hosts that used the packages.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.137.53.71"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.137.53.71"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by FirstSeen desc

Miasma persistence via Windows Run key or startup written by node/npm process AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Windows-registry autostart persistence Miasma establishes, scoped to Run/RunOnce writes performed by a node/npm process or pointing at node/sync.js/temp staging. Complements the systemd/launchd/crontab variants on non-Windows. Rationale: The article states Miasma sets Windows Registry autostart keys (alongside systemd/launchd/crontab); scoping Run-key writes to a node/npm writer or node/sync.js/temp value data ties generic persistence telemetry to this specific dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/miasma-turns-trusted-npm-packages-into-persistent-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An Electron/Node desktop app (Slack, VS Code updater) legitimately writing a Run key that references node
  • A developer tool installer setting an autostart entry pointing into AppData
  • Squirrel/auto-updater frameworks writing RunOnce values
  • Legit npm global CLI wrappers referenced in a Run value
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Microsoft VS Code\", @"\slack\", @"\Programs\") and RegistryValueData has "--updated")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the Run value data — a path into Temp/AppData/.config or referencing sync.js/node with an odd script is the tell. 2) Contain: delete the autostart value, isolate the host, and check for the matching systemd miasma-monitor.service / launchd plist on non-Windows peers. 3) Hunt: pivot from the persisted binary to its C2 (85.137.53.71) and the IPFS stage-2 fetch across the estate.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
   or RegistryValueData has_any ("node","sync.js", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", "ProgramData")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where ActingProcessName has "node" or RegistryValueData has_any ("node","sync.js", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", "ProgramData")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Miasma Registry Run-Key Persistence Written by Node
id: 5f708169-1d2f-4b70-8e93-6f7081920314
description: Detects a node/npm process creating a Windows Run/RunOnce autostart value or a Run value pointing at node/sync.js/temp staging.
references:

  - https://www.ox.security/blog/asyncapi-npm-organization-compromised-2m-weekly-downloads-affected/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
logsource:
  category: registry_set
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
    TargetObject|contains: '\CurrentVersion\Run'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\CurrentVersion\Run* OR *\currentversion\run*) @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\npm.exe)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate
| regex("\\\\CurrentVersion\\\\Run", field=RegObjectName)
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm)/i OR RegStringValue=/(node|sync\.js|\\Temp\\|\\AppData\\)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, RegStringValue], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where (Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentVersion\\Run*") AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*node*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*sync.js*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\Temp\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\AppData\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*ProgramData*") by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where (Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentVersion\\Run*") AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*node*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*sync.js*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\Temp\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\\AppData\\*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*ProgramData*") by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Suspicious downloader child (powershell/cmd/curl) spawned by npm/node_modules AIExploitation Medium
Detects a package-manager or node_modules-resident process spawning a shell/downloader with network or decode indicators — the hands-on-keyboard-free execution path of the Miasma supply-chain dropper. Scoped to node/npm/yarn/pnpm parents to avoid generic shell noise. Rationale: The dropper executes at module load inside build/CI contexts; a node/npm parent spawning a downloader shell with http/ipfs/base64/-enc indicators captures the execution pivot without the excluded generic Office-spawns-script logic. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate npm postinstall/build script using curl or Invoke-WebRequest to fetch a binary dependency (e.g. node-gyp, playwright browser download)
  • A CI pipeline step where node spawns powershell to run a signed installer
  • yarn/pnpm invoking cmd to run cross-platform helper scripts with URLs
  • Certutil used benignly by a build to verify a cert chain
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","playwright","puppeteer","electron") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","github.com","nodejs.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line and the parent package/script; benign build fetches usually pull vendor CDNs, not ipfs.io or base64 blobs. 2) Contain: if the URL is ipfs.io/the CID or the payload is encoded, kill the tree and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check the same host for sync.js drop, 85.137.53.71 beacon, and autostart persistence; review the CI job that triggered the install.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\node_modules\"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","ipfs.io","DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","FromBase64String","-enc","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","npm","yarn","pnpm")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell","pwsh","cmd","curl","wget","bash","bitsadmin","certutil")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","ipfs.io","DownloadString","Invoke-WebRequest","FromBase64String","-enc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Downloader Child Spawned by npm/node Parent
id: 60819270-2e3f-4c81-9f04-70819203142a
description: Detects node/npm/yarn/pnpm spawning a shell or downloader with network/decode indicators, matching the Miasma supply-chain execution path.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages.html
  - https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/15
tags:
  - attack.t1195.001
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\wget.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'http://'
      - 'https://'
      - 'ipfs.io'
      - 'DownloadString'
      - 'Invoke-WebRequest'
      - 'FromBase64String'
      - '-enc'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\npm.exe OR *\yarn.exe OR *\pnpm.exe) @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\cmd.exe OR *\curl.exe OR *\certutil.exe OR *\bitsadmin.exe) @CommandLine:(*http://* OR *https://* OR *ipfs.io* OR *DownloadString* OR *Invoke-WebRequest* OR *FromBase64String* OR *-enc*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(node|npm|yarn|pnpm)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|cmd|curl|wget|bitsadmin|certutil)\.exe$/i
| regex("(https?://|ipfs\\.io|DownloadString|Invoke-WebRequest|FromBase64String|-enc)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*node_modules*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") AND (Processes.process="*http://*" OR Processes.process="*https://*" OR Processes.process="*ipfs.io*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*node_modules*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe") AND (Processes.process="*http://*" OR Processes.process="*https://*" OR Processes.process="*ipfs.io*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-WebRequest*" OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a") or SHA1 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a") or MD5 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a") or SHA1 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a") or MD5 in~ ("34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["34014776d3d3ff11bc4439b02fd7ac0f02a887eb3a052eeafff236e2f6db8ad1", "082d733db0687dcd768104972b065d4b58cb1e6043688c6c20fa3702337f36ab", "bfaeb987faa6de2b5a5eb63b1233d055215b09b0349a9394f2175fd7cdf385e4", "9b2e65db653ca8575c9b10eefb9a80c6006404812c2ec212bf5675e3c690233b", "d425e4583cc6185d41e95c45eda00550045a5d1919b9a012236a4520d009dbd7", "6e78713b75bd34828d49896176627f7face7aa9036cd874f2e02d9f23a9a9c71", "9e214f38537e69bf51c7fa1ddd35ae495e9cb897231ec010baf9e4f29407ee9a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network connection to Media Land bulletproof-hosting IP 194.26.25.111 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint, perimeter and cloud-network connections to/from 194.26.25.111, a Media Land BPH address named in the DOJ indictment/OFAC sanctions and independently tied to Media Land infrastructure reselling access to ransomware/Black Basta operators. Media Land hosts malware C2, ransomware data-leak sites, phishing kits and exfil servers, so any host reaching this IP is likely beaconing or staging. Rationale: Keys on the single concrete IOC in the article (194.26.25.111), confirmed as Media Land BPH infrastructure by the Disclosing.Observer data-driven reconstruction and the OFAC advisory — a direct IP match to sanctioned ransomware-hosting infra is inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0319 • https://therecord.media/us-unseals-indictment-russians-bulletproof-hosting • https://disclosing.observer/2025/11/24/bulletproof-hoster-anatomy-data-driven-reconstruction.html

  • Security scanners or attack-surface-monitoring vendors probing the /24
  • A benign service that lands on the address after IP reallocation from Media Land following the takedown
  • VPN/proxy exit-node reuse of the address by an unrelated tenant
  • Blocklist/IOC-management tooling that resolves or test-connects to the IP for validation

1) Triage: identify the initiating process/user and direction — is a workstation beaconing (outbound) or a server receiving (inbound)? Pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine/parent tree and any files written in the same window. 2) Contain: block 194.26.25.111 (and the surrounding 194.26.25.0/24) at firewall/proxy/EDR, isolate the host if an unsigned or LOLBin process made the connection, and reset credentials used on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for ransomware pre-cursors (shadow-copy deletion, mass file writes), search all telemetry for other Media Land ranges, and check whether any inbound admin logons preceded the connection.

Authentication or cloud API activity from sanctioned Media Land BPH IP 194.26.25.111 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts sign-ins, remote logons and cloud control-plane API calls sourced from 194.26.25.111, a Media Land bulletproof-hosting address under US/UK/EU sanctions. Because Media Land brokers access to ransomware and initial-access-broker operators, any valid-account authentication or AWS/Entra API call originating from this IP indicates account takeover or attacker operations from sanctioned infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the same corroborated Media Land BPH IOC (194.26.25.111) but on a distinct pivot — identity/cloud control plane rather than endpoint egress. Any valid-account or API-key use from a sanctioned bulletproof-hosting IP is a high-signal account-takeover/attacker-operations indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0319 • https://therecord.media/us-unseals-indictment-russians-bulletproof-hosting • https://disclosing.observer/2025/11/24/bulletproof-hoster-anatomy-data-driven-reconstruction.html

  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling that authenticates test accounts to observe attacker behaviour

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Two SonicWall SMA 1000 Zero-Days Exploited, One Could Enable Admin Commands

The Hacker News
2026-07-15 6 use cases 1 technique 4 kill-chain phases detected

SonicWall has warned of active exploitation of two zero-day vulnerabilities impacting Secure Mobile Access (SMA) 1000 series appliances, one of which could be exploited to achieve arbitrary command execution. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-15409 (CVSS score: 10.0) - A Server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability that a remote unauthenticated attacker could exploit to

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 phantom /__api__/login|/__api__/logout endpoints returning HTTP 200
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 AMC hotfix rollback with path-traversal name (CVE-2026-15410 RCE) · [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 conf.json injected /__api__ route (persistence / config tampering) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Two SonicWall SMA 1000 Zero-Days Exploited, One Could Enable Admin Commands
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF via /wsproxy WebSocket upgrade (HTTP 101) with host parameter
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SonicWall SMA 1000 phantom /__api__/login|/__api__/logout endpoints returning HTTP 200 AIExploitation High
Hunts the primary forensic IOC SonicWall published for CVE-2026-15409/15410 exploitation: hits to /__api__/login or /__api__/logout in the SMA appliance web access log (extraweb_access.log) that return HTTP 200. SonicWall states these URIs do not exist in a legitimate SMA configuration, so any 200 response is a near-certain exploitation artifact. Rationale: Uses SonicWall's own published IOC verbatim (/__api__/login|/__api__/logout with HTTP 200) — SonicWall explicitly states these URIs are absent from legitimate config, making a 200 response an exploitation artifact rather than a probe. Cross-checked against BleepingComputer and SonicWall's product notice. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-warns-of-sma1000-flaws-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks-patch-now/ • https://www.sonicwall.com/support/notices/product-notice-sma-1000-series-affected-by-multiple-vulnerabilities/kA1VN000001nv6D0AQ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7) replaying the published SonicWall IOC path against the appliance for detection coverage — but these normally return 404, not 200
  • SonicWall PSIRT / support engineer validating patch efficacy by probing the endpoint on a lab appliance
  • Security team running a proof-of-concept exploit against a decommissioned/test SMA to confirm exposure
  • A reverse proxy in front of the SMA rewriting URLs such that an unrelated path collides with /__api__/ (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.0/8") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","Rapid7"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full extraweb_access.log lines for the SrcIpAddr, confirm HTTP 200 (not 404) and capture the User-Agent and any /wsproxy hits from the same source. Check whether /var/lib/unit/conf.json now contains /__api__ routes. 2) CONTAIN: Per SonicWall guidance, isolate the appliance, re-image physical or redeploy virtual SMA, then reset ALL user and admin passwords and re-provision TOTP tokens (attackers can forge sessions). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source IP across firewall/VPN logs for lateral movement, review ctrl-service.log for hotfix-rollback path-traversal entries, and enumerate any accounts created or config changes made after the first 200 response.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has_any ("/__api__/login", "/__api__/logout")
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), UserAgents=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpStatusCode
| order by LastSeen desc

SonicWall SMA 1000 SSRF via /wsproxy WebSocket upgrade (HTTP 101) with host parameter AICommand & Control High
Hunts CVE-2026-15409 (CVSS 10.0 SSRF) exploitation: requests to /wsproxy in extraweb_access.log carrying a suspicious host parameter and returning HTTP 101 (Switching Protocols). The wsproxy endpoint is abused to force the unauthenticated appliance to open a WebSocket to an attacker-chosen internal/external host. Rationale: Directly encodes SonicWall's second published IOC — /wsproxy + suspicious host parameter + HTTP 101 — which maps to the CVE-2026-15409 SSRF primitive (forcing the appliance to proxy a WebSocket to an unintended host). The host= filter isolates the SSRF target-selection parameter from benign wsproxy traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-warns-of-sma1000-flaws-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks-patch-now/ • https://securityonline.info/sonicwall-sma1000-ssrf/ • https://labs.beazley.security/advisories/BSL-A1189
ATT&CKT1090 T1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SMA WebSocket tunnels for published internal web apps that also carry a host parameter (baseline the known-good host values)
  • SonicWall NetExtender / Connect Tunnel clients establishing expected wsproxy sessions to sanctioned back-end hosts
  • Internal red-team validating CVE-2026-15409 against a lab appliance
  • Uptime/health monitors probing the wsproxy endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not (Url has_any ("host=127.0.0.1", "host=localhost") or SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Extract the decoded host= value from the /wsproxy query string — if it points at cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), an internal admin service, or an external attacker host, treat as confirmed SSRF. Correlate the SrcIpAddr with any /__api__ 200 hits. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the SMA, block the source IP at the perimeter, and follow SonicWall's re-image/redeploy + credential/TOTP reset guidance. 3) HUNT: Review the appliance's own outbound connections (firewall egress) to the host values seen in the parameter, and check internal targets for follow-on access originating from the appliance IP.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has "/wsproxy"
| where HttpStatusCode == 101
| where Url has "host="
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Targets=make_set(Url, 20) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by LastSeen desc

SonicWall SMA 1000 AMC hotfix rollback with path-traversal name (CVE-2026-15410 RCE) AIInstallation High
Hunts CVE-2026-15410 post-auth code injection: ctrl-service.log entries recording a hotfix rollback whose name contains path-traversal sequences. SonicWall lists this as a direct IOC — the Appliance Management Console rollback routine is abused to write/execute attacker content and run OS commands as administrator. Rationale: Encodes SonicWall's third IOC verbatim (ctrl-service.log hotfix rollback with path-traversal names) which is the file-system primitive behind the CVE-2026-15410 admin command-injection. Path-traversal tokens in a rollback name have no legitimate cause. Cross-checked against Help Net Security and SonicWall's notice. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/ • https://www.sonicwall.com/support/notices/product-notice-sma-1000-series-affected-by-multiple-vulnerabilities/kA1VN000001nv6D0AQ • https://securityaffairs.com/195364/hacking/sonicwall-warns-of-active-exploitation-of-two-sma-1000-zero-days.html
ATT&CKT1059 T1548 T1083
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SonicWall hotfix apply/rollback during patching that happens to log a relative path (verify the name contains ../ traversal, not just a relative filename)
  • SonicWall support engineer performing a supported rollback during a support case
  • A malformed but benign hotfix filename produced by a staging/build artifact
  • Log-forwarder re-parsing/replaying old ctrl-service.log lines after a config change
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full ctrl-service.log entry — resolve the traversal target path and identify which admin account/session triggered the rollback; correlate to any preceding /__api__ or /wsproxy hits from the same window. 2) CONTAIN: Treat as full appliance compromise with admin-level RCE — isolate, re-image physical or redeploy virtual SMA, reset all user/admin credentials and TOTP tokens per SonicWall. 3) HUNT: Enumerate files written/modified on the appliance after the rollback timestamp, review /var/lib/unit/conf.json for injected /__api__ routes, and check for new local accounts, cron/startup script changes, and outbound connections from the appliance.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessName has "ctrl-service" or SyslogMessage has "ctrl-service"
| where SyslogMessage has "hotfix" and SyslogMessage has_any ("rollback", "roll-back")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("../", "..%2f", "..%2F", "%2e%2e", @"..\")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Events=count(), Sample=make_set(SyslogMessage, 10) by Computer, HostIP
| order by LastSeen desc

SonicWall SMA 1000 conf.json injected /__api__ route (persistence / config tampering) AIInstallation High
Hunts SonicWall's config-file IOC: /var/lib/unit/conf.json (the NGINX Unit config) containing routes for /__api__/login or /__api__/logout. SonicWall states these routes do not exist in a legitimate configuration, so their presence is a durable post-exploitation persistence/backdoor artifact rather than a transient request. Rationale: Uses SonicWall's fourth published IOC — /var/lib/unit/conf.json containing /__api__ routes — which is the persistent NGINX Unit config backdoor that gives the phantom endpoints in UC1 their 200 responses. SonicWall explicitly states these routes are absent from legitimate config, making this a zero-FP structural indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/sonicwall-warns-of-sma1000-flaws-exploited-in-zero-day-attacks-patch-now/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/ • https://www.sonicwall.com/support/notices/product-notice-sma-1000-series-affected-by-multiple-vulnerabilities/kA1VN000001nv6D0AQ
ATT&CKT1556 T1505.003 T1136
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • FIM re-baselining conf.json after a legitimate SonicWall firmware upgrade that reshaped the Unit config (verify the /__api__ routes specifically, not just any conf.json change)
  • Backup/restore of a previously-compromised conf.json snapshot re-triggering the alert
  • A local IR analyst manually opening conf.json during triage, generating a file-access event
  • Non-production lab appliance intentionally seeded with the IOC for detection testing
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve the conf.json content and confirm the injected /__api__/login or /__api__/logout route block; note the modification timestamp and the account/process that last wrote the file. 2) CONTAIN: This is confirmed persistence — the appliance is compromised. Re-image physical or redeploy virtual SMA from a known-clean image (do NOT just delete the route), then reset all user/admin passwords and TOTP tokens. 3) HUNT: Correlate the conf.json write time back to the exploitation window (UC1/UC2/UC3 hits), enumerate all other appliance config/file changes since that time, and audit authentication logs for sessions that used the phantom endpoints.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "conf.json" or SyslogMessage has "/var/lib/unit"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/__api__/login", "/__api__/logout")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Events=count(), Sample=make_set(SyslogMessage, 10) by Computer, HostIP, ProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

SonicWall SMA1000 SSRF: phantom /__api__/login|logout (HTTP 200) and /wsproxy (HTTP 101) requests AIExploitation High
Hunts the initial-access footprint of CVE-2026-15409 exploitation on SMA1000 appliances: requests to /__api__/login or /__api__/logout that return HTTP 200, and /wsproxy websocket upgrades returning HTTP 101. SonicWall states these URIs do not exist on a clean appliance, so any successful hit is a compromise indicator, not benign traffic. Rationale: Uses the vendor-confirmed non-existent URIs /__api__/login, /__api__/logout (HTTP 200) and /wsproxy (HTTP 101 websocket upgrade) from the SonicWall advisory - any successful response is high-fidelity because these paths are absent from legitimate SMA1000 configurations. Cross-checked against: • https://psirt.global.sonicwall.com/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/sonicwall-sma1000-0-day-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1090.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test or vulnerability scan of the appliance deliberately probing these URIs (would still be a real 200/101 - correlate with change-management ticket)
  • A misconfigured upstream load balancer or reverse proxy rewriting health-check paths onto /wsproxy
  • Log-parser mis-extracting the status code from a non-standard access-log format, producing false 200/101 values
  • Replayed archived logs from a previously-compromised appliance being re-ingested
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the source IP is external/untrusted and that the appliance is a genuinely unpatched SMA1000 (below 12.4.3-03453 / 12.5.0-02835). Pull the full extraweb_access.log lines around the hit to see the sequence of /__api__/* and /wsproxy calls. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the appliance from the internet (block WAN mgmt/Work Place access), and begin the vendor-mandated response - re-image physical or redeploy virtual appliance, since these flaws have no workaround. Step 3 (hunt): Check /var/lib/unit/conf.json for injected /__api__ routes and ctrl-service.log for path-traversal hotfix rollbacks; rotate all user/admin passwords and reset TOTP tokens.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/__api__/login", "/__api__/logout", "/wsproxy")
| extend ReqUri = extract(@'"[A-Z]+\s+(\S+)\s+HTTP', 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend HttpStatus = toint(extract(@'HTTP/\d\.\d"?\s+(\d{3})', 1, SyslogMessage))
| where (ReqUri in ("/__api__/login","/__api__/logout") and HttpStatus == 200)
    or (ReqUri startswith "/wsproxy" and HttpStatus == 101)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, ReqUri, HttpStatus, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA1000 backdoor: rogue /__api__/login|logout routes injected into NGINX Unit conf.json AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence artifact from SMA1000 compromise: rogue HTTP route definitions for /__api__/login or /__api__/logout written into the NGINX Unit configuration at /var/lib/unit/conf.json. SonicWall confirms these route URIs never appear in a legitimate appliance config, so their presence in the config file is a durable-backdoor indicator. Rationale: Pins on the vendor IOC that /var/lib/unit/conf.json containing /__api__/login or /__api__/logout routes is illegitimate; combining the exact config path with the never-legitimate route strings makes this a low-FP persistence indicator. Telemetry depends on the appliance forwarding config/auditd events, so it is a hunt where FIM is present. Cross-checked against: • https://psirt.global.sonicwall.com/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SonicWall hotfix/patch install rewriting conf.json (would NOT add /__api__/login|logout routes - the route strings are the discriminator)
  • Vendor support session regenerating the Unit config during troubleshooting
  • Backup/restore of the appliance config replaying an older conf.json into logs
  • Config-diff tooling echoing the full conf.json (including the malicious routes) into an audit log after the appliance was already flagged
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Retrieve /var/lib/unit/conf.json from the appliance and confirm a route block referencing /__api__/login or /__api__/logout exists - these are never present in a clean config. Cross-check timestamps against extraweb_access.log SSRF hits and ctrl-service.log rollbacks. Step 2 (contain): Treat the appliance as fully compromised - take it offline, then re-image (physical) or redeploy (virtual) per SonicWall guidance; do not attempt to hand-edit conf.json. Step 3 (hunt): Reset all user and admin passwords and TOTP tokens, review VPN session logs for external admin logons, and sweep other appliances in the fleet for the same conf.json routes.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/var/lib/unit/conf.json"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/__api__/login", "/__api__/logout")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

SonicWall SMA1000 code injection: hotfix rollback with path-traversal artifact names in ctrl-service.log AIExploitation High
Hunts CVE-2026-15410 post-auth OS-command execution on SMA1000: the code-injection flaw manifests as hotfix-rollback operations in ctrl-service.log whose target/artifact names contain path-traversal sequences (../). Legitimate rollbacks never reference traversal paths, so these entries evidence both arbitrary command execution and hotfix-downgrade defense evasion. Rationale: Combines the vendor IOC 'hotfix rollbacks with path traversal names in ctrl-service.log' - the rollback keyword plus a ../ traversal sequence is the observable signature of CVE-2026-15410 command injection, and legitimate rollbacks never carry traversal artifact names, keeping FPs low. Cross-checked against: • https://psirt.global.sonicwall.com/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/14/sonicwall-sma-attacks-via-cve-2026-15409-cve-2026-15410/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/sonicwall-sma1000-0-day-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine SonicWall hotfix rollback during supported downgrade (references a normal versioned artifact name, no ../ sequence)
  • A log line quoting a user-supplied filename that innocently contains .. (rare in ctrl-service context)
  • Automated patch tooling logging relative paths that resolve within the intended directory
  • Re-ingested historical ctrl-service.log from an appliance already known-compromised
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has "rollback" and SyslogMessage has_any ("12.4.3-03453","12.5.0-02835") and not (SyslogMessage has_any ("../","..%2f","..%5c")))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the offending ctrl-service.log lines and confirm the rollback target/artifact name contains a ../ (or encoded) traversal sequence and correlate the timestamp with any /__api__ SSRF hits and conf.json changes. Verify the appliance hotfix version was downgraded to a vulnerable release. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the appliance and initiate re-image/redeploy - a traversal rollback means arbitrary command execution occurred and the appliance state cannot be trusted. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all commands run around the rollback, review admin console auth for the account that authenticated (CVE-2026-15410 is post-auth), rotate credentials/TOTP, and check the fleet for the same rollback pattern.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessName has "ctrl-service" or SyslogMessage has "ctrl-service" or SyslogMessage has "hotfix"
| where SyslogMessage has "rollback"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("../", "..%2f", "..%5c", @"..\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(_raw) as sample_events by host source
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

FacturaScripts upload endpoint: path-traversal sequence in multipart filename AIExploitation Medium
Hunts authenticated POSTs to FacturaScripts /api/3/uploadfiles or /api/3/attachedfiles where the request carries directory-traversal sequences (../, ..%2f, ..%5c) — the article's exact primitive for escaping MyFiles/ via the unsanitized getClientOriginalName() filename. Article-specific because legitimate FacturaScripts uploads never contain traversal syntax in the client filename. Rationale: Uses the article's named sinks (/api/3/uploadfiles, /api/3/attachedfiles) plus the ../ traversal signature that escapes MyFiles/. Note the traversal lives in the multipart Content-Disposition filename, not the URL — reliable only where a WAF/proxy inspects the body (CommonSecurityLog) or access logs capture request bodies; hence the companion file-write UCs. Defender XDR has no web-access-log table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Burp/Acunetix) probing the FacturaScripts upload endpoints with traversal payloads
  • Authorized pentest engagement replaying this exact GHSA PoC
  • WAF false-positive matching literal '..' in a benign filename such as 'report..final.pdf'
  • Backup/sync tooling posting archive paths containing relative segments
Suppression filter
| where user!="" and NOT match(coalesce(http_user_agent,""),"(?i)(nessus|acunetix|nuclei|burp|zgrab|nmap)")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the alerting SourceIP — confirm the multipart filename contains ../ and identify the authenticated user/API token; check the HTTP response code (2xx = write likely succeeded). 2) Contain: revoke the offending API token/session and block the SourceIP at the WAF; snapshot Dinamic/Assets/ and node_modules/ for forensics before cleanup. 3) Hunt: pivot to the file-write and .htaccess-chain UCs on the same host/time window; enumerate any .php/.phtml/.htaccess written under Dinamic/Assets or node_modules and any subsequent GET to those paths returning PHP-executed output.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("uploadfiles","attachedfiles") or Message has_any ("uploadfiles","attachedfiles")
| where RequestURL has_any ("../","..%2f","..%5c","..\\") or Message has_any ("../","..%2f","..%5c","Path Traversal","directory traversal")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

FacturaScripts: PHP/.htaccess web-shell written into web-served Dinamic/Assets or node_modules AIInstallation High
Hunts the file-write outcome of the traversal: the web-server user creating a PHP-family file or an .htaccess override inside Dinamic/Assets/ or node_modules/ — the two directories the shipped htaccess-sample excludes from index.php rewriting, so Apache serves them directly. These paths should never receive attacker-controlled executable content in normal operation. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact web-served directories (Dinamic/Assets, node_modules) combined with the BLOCKED_EXTENSIONS-bypassing extensions (.htaccess plus php-family) and a web-server initiating process. A PHP or .htaccess file appearing in these asset dirs written by httpd/php/nginx is the traversal primitive landing on disk. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/facturascripts/facturascripts/CVE-2026-27891/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FacturaScripts plugin install/update writing bundled PHP assets into Dinamic/
  • npm install/build repopulating node_modules with vendored .php or .htaccess sample files
  • Deployment/CI pipeline syncing application code into the web root
  • Developer manually copying a debugging PHP file into an assets folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","git.exe","msiexec.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","composer install","git checkout"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written file's content and hash (SHA256) — confirm it is PHP code or an AddType/AddHandler .htaccess rather than a benign asset; note the InitiatingProcess and account. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the file, take the web app offline or drop a Deny-from-all rule over Dinamic/Assets, and rotate the web-server user's credentials/API tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate with the upload-endpoint UC for the originating request, look for a second dropped payload plus subsequent inbound GETs to the file path, and scan the whole web root for other newly-created php/htaccess files by the same process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has "Dinamic" and FolderPath has "Assets") or FolderPath has "node_modules"
| extend Ext = tolower(tostring(split(FileName, ".")[-1]))
| where Ext in ("php","php3","php4","php5","php7","php8","pht","phtml","phps","phar","htaccess")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd.exe","apache.exe","apache2","httpd","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","nginx.exe","caddy.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, Ext, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where Ext in ("php","php3","php4","php5","php7","php8","pht","phtml","phps","phar","htaccess")

FacturaScripts RCE chain: .htaccess handler-remap override plus payload drop in same asset dir AIExploitation High
Detects the article's Step-3 code-execution chain on the endpoint: an attacker-written .htaccess (remapping a benign extension to the PHP handler) landing in Dinamic/Assets or node_modules, immediately followed by a second file (the payload) in the same web-served directory. The .htaccess override in these Apache-direct-served folders is essentially never legitimate and is the linchpin that turns arbitrary write into RCE. Rationale: Chains the two writes the advisory's Step 3 spells out (upload .htaccess with AddType application/x-httpd-php, then upload x.png payload) into a single temporal correlation within a web-served asset dir — far higher fidelity than either write alone. The Falcon variant isolates the .htaccess override linchpin that uniquely enables the extension remap. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hgjx-r89m-m7v4 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vf3q-frmr-vrr9
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • FacturaScripts/plugin installer laying down a directory-level .htaccess alongside static files
  • CI artifact extraction writing an .htaccess and multiple assets together
  • Admin manually hardening an asset directory by dropping a Deny .htaccess next to existing files

Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .htaccess contents (look for AddType/AddHandler/SetHandler mapping a non-PHP extension to php) and inspect the paired payload file for PHP code; capture the initiating web-server account. 2) Contain: delete both files, take the site offline or override the directory with Deny-from-all, and rotate the web-server user credentials and any upload-capable API tokens. 3) Hunt: review web logs for inbound GETs to the payload path (successful RCE trigger), check for outbound C2 from the web-server process, and sweep the entire document root for other .htaccess overrides written by the same process.

Exposure hunt: hosts still vulnerable to actively-exploited July 2026 zero-days (AD FS CVE-2026-56155 / SharePoint CVE-2026-56164) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed asset whose vulnerability inventory still lists the two July-2026 Patch Tuesday zero-days Microsoft flagged as exploited in the wild — the AD FS EoP (CVE-2026-56155) and the SharePoint Server missing-auth EoP (CVE-2026-56164). Article-specific because it pins on the exact CVE IDs Microsoft confirmed under active attack, letting the SOC prioritise emergency patching of AD FS and SharePoint farms over the other 568 fixes. Rationale: Pins on the two CVE IDs the article explicitly names as actively exploited (CVE-2026-56155 AD FS EoP, CVE-2026-56164 SharePoint EoP) — matched against Microsoft's own MDVM CVE catalog, so it is self-corroborating and hand-edit-free.
ATT&CKT1068 T1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A host was patched but TVM inventory hasn't re-scanned yet (stale RecommendedSecurityUpdate)
  • Out-of-band build number that Microsoft's detection logic flags conservatively
  • Decommissioned AD FS/SharePoint server still reporting old inventory
  • Third-party scanner mapping the CVE to an unaffected SKU
  • Air-gapped server where the July cumulative update was applied offline but not reflected in the feed
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): confirm the asset is genuinely internet-reachable or business-critical (AD FS proxy, SharePoint front-end) and that the installed KB predates the July 2026 cumulative update. Step 2 (contain): apply the July CU immediately; for SharePoint, as an interim mitigation enable AMSI with Request Body Scan mode = Full per Microsoft guidance; for AD FS, restrict local logon and review admin group membership. Step 3 (hunt): on any host that was unpatched, pivot to UC2 (w3wp spawning shells) and review AD FS admin-role changes and new service accounts around the exposure window.

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning a command interpreter — post-exploitation of CVE-2026-56164 AIExploitation Medium
Detects a SharePoint application-pool worker process (w3wp.exe) spawning cmd/powershell/net/whoami and other interpreters — the classic hands-on-keyboard footprint after a SharePoint privilege-escalation/missing-auth exploit like the actively-exploited CVE-2026-56164. Article-specific because it targets the SharePoint zero-day Microsoft confirmed under attack this Patch Tuesday, scoping the parent to SharePoint app pools rather than generic IIS. Rationale: Scopes to the SharePoint zero-day (CVE-2026-56164) Microsoft confirmed as actively exploited by pivoting on the SharePoint app-pool worker (w3wp.exe with 'SharePoint' in its app-pool command line) spawning interpreters — a high-fidelity hands-on-keyboard signal not covered by the excluded Office-spawns-script rule.
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health jobs invoking PowerShell for farm maintenance
  • Admin using stsadm/PowerShell SharePoint management shell under the app-pool identity during a change window
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM) shelling out from the IIS worker
  • Deployment automation running net.exe/whoami for post-deploy validation
  • Custom SharePoint solution legitimately shelling out (rare, should be baselined)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("stsadm","Microsoft.SharePoint.PowerShell","OWSTIMER") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for recon (whoami/net group), download cradles, or web-shell writes; confirm the w3wp identity and whether a change window is active. Step 2 (contain): isolate the SharePoint front-end, kill the offending process tree, and capture w3wp memory; verify the July CU / AMSI Full-body-scan mitigation is applied. Step 3 (hunt): search DeviceFileEvents for newly written .aspx/.ashx under the SharePoint LAYOUTS/TEMPLATE web-accessible paths, review IIS logs for the triggering request, and pivot on any accounts/keys created after the first shell.

TidGi Desktop wiki worker spawning a command interpreter (TiddlyWiki startup-module RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payload of GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv: after a malicious TiddlyWiki repo is imported, an auto-registered `module-type: startup` tiddler executes `require('child_process').execSync(...)` inside the TidGi Node.js wiki-worker thread, spawning a shell/LOLBin. A knowledge-management wiki app spawning cmd/powershell is anomalous and directly evidences exploitation. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit mechanics from the advisory (startup-module auto-exec calling require('child_process').execSync inside the TidGi wiki-worker) — a wiki app parenting cmd/powershell/LOLBins is high-fidelity. Cross-checked DeepWiki (worker-thread architecture runs in-process, so InitiatingProcess=TidGi.exe) and MITRE T1218.015. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9hc2-hjx8-q6pv • https://deepwiki.com/tiddly-gittly/TidGi-Desktop/3.1-wiki-worker-and-nodejs-tiddlywiki • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/015/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059 T1218.015

  • A legitimately-installed TiddlyWiki plugin that intentionally shells out to a system tool
  • TidGi feature that opens an external file/URL via a helper that transits cmd.exe
  • Unrelated node.exe located in a folder path coincidentally containing the string 'TidGi'
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "cmd.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","--git-dir","rev-parse"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ProcessCommandLine and TidGi's InitiatingProcessCommandLine; benign hits are usually git/backup helpers (excluded) — attacker payloads show execSync-style `cmd /c` with attacker commands. Identify the workspace folder and the most recently added tiddlers/*.js.tid file. 2) Contain: kill the TidGi and child process tree, isolate the host, and quarantine the imported wiki workspace directory to prevent re-boot re-execution. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for follow-on child processes, outbound connections from TidGi.exe, and any git.exe clone that delivered the repo; check other users who imported the same repo/URL.
