LabubaRAT user-level autostart persistence (Run key / scheduled task referencing NVIDIA loader) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Run/RunOnce registry writes or scheduled-task creation that reference the LabubaRAT loader (nvidia-sysruntime) or its C2 (pipicka.xyz), or that are written by an nvidia-named process — the 'user level autostart' persistence the article says LabubaRAT maintains. Rationale: Article explicitly notes LabubaRAT maintains 'user level autostart'; keying Run-key value data on the named loader and pipicka.xyz IOC keeps this tight while the nvidia-writer clause catches renamed variants. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine NVIDIA GeForce Experience / driver auto-update writing an nvidia Run entry from \Program Files\NVIDIA
  • Software-deployment tooling staging an nvidia launcher in Run for post-reboot install
  • Backup/imaging solution restoring a legacy Run value
  • Analyst re-adding a known-good nvidia autostart during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where not(RegistryValueData has "\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or RegistryValueData has "\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Run value data and confirm the referenced binary is the unsigned nvidia-sysruntime loader (not \Program Files\NVIDIA). 2) Contain: delete the autostart value/task, quarantine the referenced binary, isolate host. 3) Hunt: check for the same value across the fleet and correlate with pipicka.xyz beaconing and loader execution.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime" or RegistryValueData has "pipicka.xyz" or (InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "nvidia-sysruntime" or RegistryValueData has "pipicka.xyz" or ActingProcessName contains "\\nvidia"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized NVIDIA installer download from non-NVIDIA source AIDelivery Medium
Hunts creation/download of an nvidia-named executable whose mark-of-the-web origin URL is NOT an NVIDIA domain, or that is written to disk by a browser/mail client — the delivery vector for the fake NVIDIA container-runtime installer that drops LabubaRAT. Rationale: The 'masquerades as NVIDIA software' premise implies a fake installer; keying an nvidia-named exe on a non-NVIDIA origin URL (mark-of-the-web) or a browser/mail-client writer surfaces the delivery without alerting on legitimate NVIDIA downloads. Sigma/Datadog omitted because origin-URL is not a standard field for those log shapes. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002 T1036
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Users downloading NVIDIA drivers from a legitimate mirror/CDN not on the allowlist (e.g. an OEM or Steam-hosted redistributable)
  • Internal software portal re-hosting NVIDIA installers on a corporate URL
  • Driver-management tools (Snappy/Chocolatey) fetching nvidia packages
  • Archived nvidia installer copied from a file share and re-tagged with a referrer URL

| where not(FileOriginUrl has_any ("chocolatey.org","steamstatic.com") or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull FileOriginUrl + referrer and SHA256; confirm the source domain is attacker-controlled and the file is unsigned/non-NVIDIA. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the source domain at the proxy, and check whether it was executed. 3) Hunt: search EmailUrlInfo/EmailAttachmentInfo for the same lure, and sweep the fleet for the hash plus subsequent nvidia-sysruntime.exe execution and pipicka.xyz traffic.

| where isnotempty(FileOriginUrl)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

NVIDIA-branded process outbound to non-NVIDIA public infrastructure (LabubaRAT C2 / SOCKS5 proxy) AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioral C2 hunt: any nvidia-named process making public network connections to destinations that are NOT NVIDIA infrastructure. Catches LabubaRAT's HTTPS/WebView2 C2 and SOCKS5 proxy traffic even when the operator swaps out pipicka.xyz for fresh infrastructure (the article stresses the binary is re-tasked per campaign). Rationale: Behavioral complement to the pipicka.xyz IOC hunt: legitimate NVIDIA software talks only to NVIDIA/CDN infrastructure, so an nvidia-named process reaching arbitrary public IPs/domains captures LabubaRAT's re-taskable HTTPS/WebView2 C2 and SOCKS5 proxying. Sentinel left blank — this tenant's Sentinel network tables (ImNetworkSession/CommonSecurityLog) don't carry the initiating process image needed to bind the connection to nvidia*.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/new-rust-based-rat-named-labubarat-impersonates-nvidia-software
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • NVIDIA software contacting a licensing/telemetry endpoint on a non-nvidia.com CDN (Akamai/Cloudflare edge)
  • GeForce Experience pulling game-ready driver assets from a third-party CDN
  • OEM nvidia utility phoning home to the OEM's domain
  • Crash-reporter uploading to a non-NVIDIA error-aggregation service
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files\\NVIDIA" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\NVIDIA")
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the remote IP/domain and check reputation/passive-DNS; confirm the initiating binary is the unsigned nvidia-sysruntime loader and assess connection periodicity for beaconing. 2) Contain: block the destination, isolate the host, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: pivot the destination IP across the fleet, correlate with pipicka.xyz DNS, Run-key persistence, and loader execution; review for SOCKS5 listener/relay behavior.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "nvidia" and InitiatingProcessFileName endswith ".exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteUrl has "nvidia.com" or RemoteUrl has "nvidia.cn" or RemoteUrl endswith "nvidia.co")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc

| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| summarize qcount = count(), uniqueSubs = dcount(RemoteUrl), maxLabel = max(qlen)
    by DeviceName, SecondLevelDomain
| where qcount > 100 and uniqueSubs > 20

            by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)

Miggo's security team, which discovered and reported the flaws, said one "leaks the broker's confidential OAuth

Unauthenticated GET /api/auth on RabbitMQ management port leaking OAuth client secret (CVE-2026-57219) AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to the obsolete RabbitMQ management HTTP endpoint GET /api/auth on port 15672, which returns the broker's OAuth client secret to any unauthenticated caller. Focuses on external/untrusted source IPs hitting the exact path, since the endpoint's authz check was hard-coded to always allow. Rationale: Pivots on the exact obsolete path '/api/auth' plus the RabbitMQ management port 15672 named in the disclosure; because every other sensitive management endpoint requires auth, GET /api/auth returning 200 is a near-unique high-fidelity signal.
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate RabbitMQ management UI automation/health checks polling /api/ endpoints from internal monitoring hosts
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) probing /api/auth during authorized scans
  • Internal admin browsing the management UI whose session hits /api/auth
  • Load balancer health probes configured against the management API
Suppression filter
| where not (ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr)) and HttpStatusCode == 200
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the requesting SrcIpAddr is external/untrusted and the response status was 200 (secret returned); check whether the instance uses management.oauth_client_secret. 2) Contain: block port 15672 from untrusted networks, patch to 4.3.0/4.2.6/4.1.11/4.0.20/3.13.15, and immediately rotate the OAuth client secret. 3) Hunt: search AAD/OAuth token issuance and RabbitMQ admin API calls from the leaked secret for follow-on admin-token exchange and queue/user/config changes.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| where Url has "/api/auth"
| where DstPortNumber == 15672 or Url has ":15672"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cross-tenant RabbitMQ queue/exchange enumeration via management API (CVE-2026-57221) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single source enumerating many queue and exchange names through the RabbitMQ management API (/api/queues, /api/exchanges) on port 15672, abusing the missing authorization that lets any connected vhost user read all queue/exchange names, message counts and consumer counts regardless of permissions. Rationale: Uses the specific management API resource paths (/api/queues, /api/exchanges) and port 15672 tied to the missing-authz flaw; a source pulling >20 distinct queue/exchange paths in a short window is the enumeration behaviour the CVE enables, whereas normal management UI use touches few endpoints.
ATT&CKT1087 T1580
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • RabbitMQ management UI overview page auto-refreshing and paging through the full queue/exchange list for a legitimate admin
  • Monitoring exporters (rabbitmq_exporter / Prometheus) scraping /api/queues and /api/exchanges on a schedule
  • Capacity/inventory tooling walking all vhosts for reporting
  • CI pipelines validating broker topology across many queues
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("monitoring-host-ip-not-known") and not (ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) and DstHostname has "exporter")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the authenticated user behind SrcIpAddr and compare their assigned vhost permissions to the breadth of queues/exchanges enumerated; legit monitoring accounts are expected, ad-hoc user accounts are not. 2) Contain: restrict port 15672 to trusted management networks, separate tenants by vhost, and patch to the fixed release lines. 3) Hunt: review whether the same principal then consumed messages or authenticated to queues outside its tenant, and correlate with any /api/auth secret-leak hits.

| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where HttpMethod == "GET"
| where DstPortNumber == 15672 or Url has ":15672"
| where Url has_any ("/api/queues", "/api/exchanges")

| order by DistinctPaths desc

11 Old Microsoft-Signed Linux UEFI Shims Could Let Attackers Bypass Secure Boot

The Hacker News
2026-07-14 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered 11 old, Microsoft-signed, Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) applications that could be abused to bypass Secure Boot on most systems using the modern firmware standard. "An attacker exploiting one of these vulnerable applications can execute untrusted code during system boot, enabling deployment of malicious UEFI bootkits or other malware,"

Revoked Microsoft-signed vulnerable UEFI shim present in estate (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797) AIInstallation High
Surfaces hosts carrying one of the 11 old Microsoft-signed shim bootloaders (shim 0.9 and earlier) revoked in Microsoft's June 2026 DBX update. Any device still exposing CVE-2026-8863 or CVE-2026-10797 can be used to bypass UEFI Secure Boot by bringing the still-trusted-but-unrevoked binary, so this is an exposure hunt, not a live-exploit alert. Rationale: Uses the two concrete CVE IDs assigned to the 11 revoked shims (confirmed by ESET/CERT). A pure inventory lookup — zero behavioural noise, ideal for prioritising DBX/fwupd remediation on Linux fleets that trust the Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 cert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/457458 • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1553.006
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped/offline lab boxes intentionally kept on old shims for reproduction
  • Appliances (Blancco WipeDrive / PC-Doctor / baramundi) that legitimately ship the affected shim as designed
  • Hosts pending a scheduled fwupd/DBX maintenance window
  • Golden images not yet re-baked after the June 2026 revocation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device trusts the Microsoft 3rd-party CA and check `mokutil --sb-state` and DBX entry count (`efi-readvar -v dbx | grep -c sha256`, expect 200+). 2) Contain: push the Microsoft June-2026 DBX/fwupd revocation update or apply the SBAT level bump so the old shim can no longer load; prioritise internet-facing and privileged-user hosts. 3) Hunt: on any host that resisted DBX update, pivot to UC2/UC3 to check whether the ESP shim was actually swapped or MOK/SBAT validation was disabled.

Old shim/GRUB EFI binary written to ESP by non-package-manager process (Secure Boot bypass staging) AIInstallation Medium
Detects writes of a shim, MokManager or GRUB EFI binary into the EFI System Partition by a process that is NOT a legitimate package manager / firmware updater. This is the core of the attack: replacing the victim's up-to-date shim with an older, still-Microsoft-signed vulnerable one to reintroduce a bootkit-capable early-boot code-exec path that survives OS reinstall. Rationale: Anchors on the exact ESP artifact names (shimx64.efi / mmx64.efi / grubx64.efi) and the /boot/efi path where an attacker swaps in the old signed shim; excluding real installers/fwupd keeps the true-positive (manual/scripted replacement) sharp. ESET's core finding is that only 'a copy of an old still-trusted shim' is needed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/457458
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1542.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro kernel/shim upgrade run via a wrapper the exclusion list misses (e.g. ansible/salt invoking cp directly)
  • Imaging/provisioning tools (baramundi, FOG) legitimately writing shim to ESP during deployment
  • Manual `cp`/`dd` by a sysadmin recovering an unbootable machine
  • Dual-boot setup utilities re-installing the EFI bootloader
  • Backup/restore agents rehydrating /boot/efi
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the written binary's SHA256 and compare against the distro's current signed shim; run `objdump -j .sbat -s <file>` — an absent/low-generation .sbat section on a freshly written shim is a strong signal of an old vulnerable build. Confirm the writing process/user was not a package transaction. 2) Contain: isolate the host, restore the vendor-current shim, and (re)apply the DBX revocation so the old binary can't load; reset boot order with efibootmgr. 3) Hunt: check UC3 for accompanying `mokutil --disable-validation`/SBAT reset, and scan other hosts for the same file hash and writing-process lineage.

| where FileName in~ ("shimx64.efi","shimaa64.efi","shimia32.efi","mmx64.efi","grubx64.efi","fbx64.efi","bootx64.efi")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","dnf","yum","zypper","zypp","fwupd","fwupdmgr","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub","packagekitd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("dpkg","rpm","apt","dnf","yum","zypper","fwupd","grub-install","grub2-install","shim-install","update-grub"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Old Vulnerable Shim/GRUB EFI Binary Written to ESP by Non-Installer
id: 5c2f8a41-9b6e-4d13-8a77-2e1c4b90d6f2
description: Detects a shim/MokManager/GRUB EFI binary written into /boot/efi by a process that is not a legitimate package manager or firmware updater, consistent with staging an older Microsoft-signed vulnerable shim to bypass Secure Boot (CVE-2026-8863 / CVE-2026-10797).
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/

  - attack.t1542.001
  - attack.defense_evasion

    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - 'shimx64.efi'

      - 'fbx64.efi'

level: high

| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\/(dpkg|rpm|apt|apt-get|dnf|yum|zypper|fwupd|fwupdmgr|grub2?-install|shim-install|update-grub)$/i

ENDPOINT

MOK/SBAT enforcement disabled via mokutil (Secure Boot validation subversion) AIInstallation Medium
Detects mokutil invocations that disable shim signature validation or roll back the SBAT revocation policy — the exact levers the article describes for bypassing MOK-denylist and SBAT enforcement so an older revoked shim will load unchallenged. Pairs with UC2 to catch the enforcement-weakening half of the chain. Rationale: The article states the bypass works by defeating MOK-denylist and SBAT enforcement; `mokutil --disable-validation` and `--set-sbat-policy` (with `--import`/`--reset`) are the precise CLI levers to do that (corroborated by shim/mokutil docs). Named binary + dangerous flags keeps it targeted rather than a generic 'mokutil ran' dashboard. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/forgotten-uefi-shims-undermining-secure-boot/ • https://kb.cert.org/vuls/id/616257
ATT&CKT1553.006 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin enrolling a new MOK for a third-party/DKMS driver (`mokutil --import`)
  • Sanctioned SBAT policy rollback during a distro-support troubleshooting case
  • NVIDIA/VirtualBox/DKMS module signing workflows on first install
  • Golden-image build pipelines enrolling keys before hardening
  • Lab/test hosts where an engineer disabled validation intentionally
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("dkms","akmods","packagekitd") and ProcessCommandLine has "--import")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the invoking user/parent is an expected admin/automation account and whether a DKMS/third-party driver install is in flight; `--disable-validation` and SBAT `--reset` outside a change window are the red flags. 2) Contain: re-enable validation (`mokutil --enable-validation`), restore the current SBAT level, and revoke any unexpected enrolled MOK; isolate if paired with an ESP shim write (UC2). 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for a recent shim/GRUB EFI write (UC2), new efibootmgr boot-order changes, and reboots shortly after; sweep the fleet for the same command lineage.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mokutil"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--disable-validation", "--set-sbat-policy", "--import", "--reset")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "mokutil"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--disable-validation", "--set-sbat-policy", "--import", "--reset")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

OAuth Client ID Spoofing Lets Attackers Validate Stolen Microsoft Entra Credentials

The Hacker News
2026-07-14 5 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

At least two distinct threat actors are weaponizing a novel evasion technique called OAuth client ID spoofing in cloud campaigns, while slipping past telemetry. The activity allows users to enumerate user accounts and validate stolen credentials in Microsoft Entra ID environments, without ever generating a successful sign-in event that would otherwise alert defenders. And bad actors have begun

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Entra sign-in with populated OAuth client ID but blank application name (spoofed client_id)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Single source IP presenting many distinct spoofed OAuth client IDs (fragmentation to evade per-app detection) · [LLM] AADSTS700016 with blank app name — spoofed client ID confirms VALID Entra credentials
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Account-lockout burst (AADSTS50053) driven by spoofed-client-ID enumeration · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Entra sign-in with populated OAuth client ID but blank application name (spoofed client_id) AIReconnaissance High
Hunts Entra ID sign-in events where an ApplicationId/AppId is present but the application display name is blank — the exact telemetry gap Proofpoint documented for OAuth client ID spoofing via the ROPC token endpoint. Legitimate registered apps always resolve to a name; a populated GUID with no name indicates a fictional (spoofed) client ID used for stealthy account/credential enumeration. Rationale: The blank application-name-with-populated-client-ID signature is the specific evasion Proofpoint identified — surges against a named app are missed because the field is blank. Cross-checked Proofpoint, Help Net Security and CyberPress; all confirm 'sign-in log entries with blank application IDs / no application name' as the primary IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/oauth-client-id-spoofing-why-fake-client-ids-are-gaining-traction-stealthy • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/13/entra-id-oauth-client-id-spoofing/ • https://cyberpress.org/hackers-validate-entra-credentials/
ATT&CKT1087.004 T1110.003
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Orphaned app registration recently deleted while users/service accounts still authenticate against the stale AppId (blank name)
  • Transient directory-replication delay where a newly registered first-party/LOB app has not yet resolved to a display name
  • Legacy ROPC-based service accounts configured with ad-hoc client IDs
  • Third-party SDK or connector cycling client IDs during a misconfiguration
Suppression filter
| where DistinctUsers > 3   // one orphaned app hit by a single user is benign; spoofing sprays many users from one source
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending IPAddress/ApplicationId; check the ASN — Proofpoint's campaigns originated from AWS (UNK_pyreq2323) and Cloudflare (UNK_OutFlareAZ). Confirm the AppId does not match any registered app (Entra > App registrations). 2) Contain: block the source IP/ASN at Conditional Access / named-locations, force password reset for any user showing a 700016/50126 result, and enable smart lockout monitoring. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same IP for distinct-AppId fan-out (UC2), 700016 valid-credential confirmations (UC3), and lockout bursts (UC4); review whether targeted usernames follow an alphabetical wordlist pattern.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(ApplicationId)
| where isempty(AppDisplayName) and isempty(Application)
| summarize AttemptCount = count(), DistinctUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), ErrorCodes = make_set(ErrorCode, 20), Clients = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by ApplicationId, IPAddress
| where AttemptCount > 1
| order by AttemptCount desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(AppId)
| where isempty(AppDisplayName)
| summarize AttemptCount = count(), DistinctUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName), ResultCodes = make_set(ResultType, 20), Clients = make_set(ClientAppUsed, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AppId, IPAddress
| where AttemptCount > 1
| order by AttemptCount desc
title: Entra Sign-in With OAuth Client ID But Blank Application Name
id: 5f2a1c34-8e7b-4a2d-9c11-3b6f0a9e21d4
description: Detects Entra ID sign-in events carrying a populated OAuth client ID (AppId) with an empty application display name, indicating a spoofed/fictional client ID used for stealthy enumeration via the ROPC token endpoint.
references:
  - https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/oauth-client-id-spoofing-why-fake-client-ids-are-gaining-traction-stealthy
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/oauth-client-id-spoofing-lets-attackers.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:

  - attack.t1110.003
logsource:
  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  selection:
    AppId|exists: true
  filter_blank:
    AppDisplayName: ''
  condition: selection and filter_blank
level: medium
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" -@properties.appDisplayName:*
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as attempts, dc(Authentication.user) as distinct_users, values(Authentication.signature_id) as aadsts_codes, values(Authentication.action) as actions, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where nodename=Authentication (Authentication.app="" OR Authentication.app="unknown" OR Authentication.app="N/A") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where attempts>1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - attempts
| tstats summariesonly=false count as attempts, dc(Authentication.user) as distinct_users, values(Authentication.signature_id) as aadsts_codes, values(Authentication.action) as actions, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where nodename=Authentication (Authentication.app="" OR Authentication.app="unknown" OR Authentication.app="N/A") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where attempts>1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - attempts
Single source IP presenting many distinct spoofed OAuth client IDs (fragmentation to evade per-app detection) AIExploitation High
Detects one source IP submitting many distinct client IDs that all resolve to a blank application name within a short window — the fragmentation tradecraft where UNK_OutFlareAZ generated a unique UUIDv4 per request and UNK_pyreq2323 reused mutated IDs across up to 12 users. A legitimate application authenticates under exactly one stable client ID, so high AppId cardinality from a single origin is anomalous. Rationale: Directly encodes the 'fragmenting authentication across many fictional applications' behaviour Proofpoint describes (700K+ / 3.7M spoofed IDs). Distinct-AppId cardinality per source IP is the pivot that legacy per-application-name detections and CA-per-app scoping cannot see. Splunk uses a volume/user proxy because CIM Authentication has no client-ID GUID field. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/oauth-client-id-spoofing-why-fake-client-ids-are-gaining-traction-stealthy • https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-spoof-oauth-client-ids/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1087.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagement enumerating the tenant from a single jump host
  • Security scanner or attack-surface tool probing app registrations
  • Misconfigured SDK or gateway rotating client IDs on every request from a shared egress IP
  • Large corporate NAT/proxy egress aggregating many legitimate app auths behind one IP (mitigated by requiring blank app name)
Suppression filter
| where DistinctUsers >= 10   // scoped to broad user targeting; suppresses single-user SDK client-ID rotation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is not a corporate egress/proxy; check ASN for AWS/Cloudflare hosting ranges consistent with the campaigns. Review AppSample GUIDs — sequential/trailing-digit mutations (UNK_pyreq2323) or fully random UUIDv4 (UNK_OutFlareAZ) confirm spoofing. 2) Contain: block the IP/ASN via Conditional Access named locations; if any targeted user shows 700016/50126, force reset + revoke sessions. 3) Hunt: enumerate all users touched by this IP, correlate with lockout bursts (UC4), and check whether targeted UPNs are alphabetically ordered (wordlist signature).
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where isempty(AppDisplayName) and isnotempty(ApplicationId)
| summarize DistinctAppIds = dcount(ApplicationId), DistinctUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), Attempts = count(), AppSample = make_set(ApplicationId, 10) by IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctAppIds >= 10   // a real app authenticates under ONE stable client ID; 10+ fictional IDs from one source in 1h = spoofing fan-out
| order by DistinctAppIds desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where isempty(AppDisplayName) and isnotempty(AppId)
| summarize DistinctAppIds = dcount(AppId), DistinctUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Attempts = count(), AppSample = make_set(AppId, 10) by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctAppIds >= 10   // 10+ distinct spoofed client IDs from one source in 1h
| order by DistinctAppIds desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" -@properties.appDisplayName:* @properties.status.errorCode:(50126 OR 50034 OR 700016)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as attempts, dc(Authentication.user) as distinct_users, values(Authentication.signature_id) as aadsts_codes, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where nodename=Authentication (Authentication.app="" OR Authentication.app="unknown") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where attempts>=20 AND distinct_users>=10 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - attempts
| tstats summariesonly=false count as attempts, dc(Authentication.user) as distinct_users, values(Authentication.signature_id) as aadsts_codes, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where nodename=Authentication (Authentication.app="" OR Authentication.app="unknown") Authentication.action=failure by Authentication.src, _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where attempts>=20 AND distinct_users>=10 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - attempts
AADSTS700016 with blank app name — spoofed client ID confirms VALID Entra credentials AIExploitation High
Hunts sign-in events returning AADSTS700016 ('application identifier not recognized') against a blank application name. Per Proofpoint/Help Net, when a spoofed client ID yields 700016, authentication progressed far enough that only the fake app was rejected — meaning the submitted username AND password are valid. This is a credential-validation success masquerading as a benign failed login. Rationale: 700016 is the single highest-fidelity outcome of the technique — corroborating sources (Help Net, CyberPress) explicitly state it signals compromised credentials, not a benign failure. Pairing it with the blank-app-name condition isolates spoofed-client-ID validations from ordinary unknown-app errors. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/07/13/entra-id-oauth-client-id-spoofing/ • https://cyberpress.org/hackers-validate-entra-credentials/ • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/oauth-client-id-spoofing-why-fake-client-ids-are-gaining-traction-stealthy
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1110.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user with a valid password hitting a genuinely deleted/decommissioned app registration (bookmarked or cached old client ID)
  • App-migration cutover where the old registration was removed but clients still hold the old client ID
  • Internal QA/testing deliberately using an invalid client ID with real test-account credentials
Response runbook
1) Triage: treat every AccountUpn returned as a confirmed valid-credential exposure — check the source IP/ASN and whether the AppId is a spoofed GUID (no matching registration). 2) Contain: immediately force password reset and revoke refresh tokens for the listed users; require MFA/re-registration and block the source. 3) Hunt: search successful sign-ins (ErrorCode 0) for the same users post-event to detect actual account takeover, and pivot the source IP through UC1/UC2 to scope the full target list.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 700016   // app identifier not recognized, but username+password validated
| where isempty(AppDisplayName)
| summarize Hits = count(), Sources = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(ApplicationId, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn
| order by LastSeen desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where toint(ResultType) == 700016   // spoofed app rejected but credentials valid
| where isempty(AppDisplayName)
| summarize Hits = count(), Sources = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Apps = make_set(AppId, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName
| order by LastSeen desc
title: AADSTS700016 With Blank App Name Indicates Valid Entra Credentials via Spoofed Client ID

source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:700016 -@properties.appDisplayName:*
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as hits, values(Authentication.src) as src, values(Authentication.app) as app, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where nodename=Authentication Authentication.signature_id=700016 by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - hits
| tstats summariesonly=false count as hits, values(Authentication.src) as src, values(Authentication.app) as app, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where nodename=Authentication Authentication.signature_id=700016 by Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - hits
Account-lockout burst (AADSTS50053) driven by spoofed-client-ID enumeration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a surge of AADSTS50053 lockouts within a short window, weighted toward sign-ins with blank application names. Proofpoint reported UNK_pyreq2323's enumeration locked out roughly 28% of targeted users — so a mass-lockout burst that correlates with blank-app-name activity is a high-recall tripwire for this campaign even when the attacker fully randomizes client IDs to evade per-app detection. Rationale: The ~28% lockout figure is an article-specific, measurable side effect; keying the burst on the co-occurrence of blank-app-name attempts distinguishes campaign-driven lockouts from ordinary smart-lockout noise and survives full client-ID randomization. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/oauth-client-id-spoofing-why-fake-client-ids-are-gaining-traction-stealthy • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/oauth-client-id-spoofing-lets-attackers.html
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1531
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy-protocol misconfiguration (cached bad password on many mobile/Exchange ActiveSync clients) causing self-inflicted lockout waves
  • Smart-lockout threshold tuned too aggressively after a policy change
  • A genuine password-spray from a different actor (still a true positive worth escalating)
  • Post-password-reset events where fleets of devices retry stale credentials
Suppression filter
| where DistinctApps >= 5 or BlankAppAttempts >= LockedUsers   // require the spoofing signature, not a single-app misconfig lockout wave
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the lockout burst coincides with BlankAppAttempts and check the Sources ASN for AWS/Cloudflare hosting ranges. Rule out a recent org-wide password reset or ActiveSync misconfig. 2) Contain: block offending source IPs/ASN via Conditional Access; verify Smart Lockout is enabled and consider tightening named-location policy (note CA scoped per-app will NOT trigger on spoofed IDs). 3) Hunt: for every locked user, check for a preceding 700016/50126 (valid-credential) result (UC3) and any subsequent successful sign-in indicating takeover.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 50053   // account locked from repeated failed attempts
| summarize LockedUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), Attempts = count(), BlankAppAttempts = countif(isempty(AppDisplayName)), DistinctApps = dcount(ApplicationId), Sources = make_set(IPAddress, 20) by bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where LockedUsers >= 20   // mass lockout burst; campaign locked ~28% of targeted users
| where BlankAppAttempts > 0
| order by LockedUsers desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where toint(ResultType) == 50053   // account locked
| summarize LockedUsers = dcount(UserPrincipalName), Attempts = count(), BlankAppAttempts = countif(isempty(AppDisplayName)), DistinctApps = dcount(AppId), Sources = make_set(IPAddress, 20) by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where LockedUsers >= 20   // mass lockout burst consistent with enumeration campaign
| where BlankAppAttempts > 0
| order by LockedUsers desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:50053
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Authentication.user) as locked_users, count as attempts, values(Authentication.src) as src from datamodel=Authentication where nodename=Authentication Authentication.signature_id=50053 by _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where locked_users>=20 | sort - locked_users
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.user) as locked_users, count as attempts, values(Authentication.src) as src from datamodel=Authentication where nodename=Authentication Authentication.signature_id=50053 by _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where locked_users>=20 | sort - locked_users
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

The serpent’s tongue: Luring the Python out of its den

Cisco Talos
2026-07-14 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

This blog examines the full lifecycle of a Python package, from hosting on repositories such as PyPI or custom web servers, through source and wheel distribution formats, to the final installation into virtual or system-wide Python environments.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] pip install redirected to non-PyPI index / find-links (dependency confusion) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Python setup.py install-time code execution spawning shell/LOLBin · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — The serpent’s tongue: Luring the Python out of its den
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious .pth file dropped into site-packages by pip/python · [LLM] Persistent PIP_ index/config environment variable set in registry
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
pip install redirected to non-PyPI index / find-links (dependency confusion) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts pip invocations that pull packages from an --index-url / --extra-index-url / --find-links pointing anywhere other than pypi.org or files.pythonhosted.org. This is the article's 'custom web server / alternate index' hosting-layer abuse used to serve malicious packages or dependency-confusion payloads. Rationale: Anchors on the article's custom-index hosting layer using the exact pip flags (--index-url/--extra-index-url/--find-links) and excludes the two canonical PyPI hosts (pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org) the article names as the legitimate download path. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/defending_against_team_pcp_software_supply_chain_attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal corporate PyPI mirror (Artifactory/Nexus/devpi) configured via --index-url on the CLI
  • CI/CD build agents installing from a private package feed URL
  • Developers testing a local devpi/pypiserver during package development
  • Air-gapped hosts using --find-links against an offline wheelhouse directory
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("artifactory","nexus","devpi","pkgs.dev.azure.com","codeartifact","jfrog.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the index/find-links host from ProcessCommandLine; is it a known internal mirror or an external/unrecognised domain or raw IP? Check WHOIS/first-seen. 2) Contain: if the host is untrusted, isolate the endpoint, capture the pip cache and any newly created site-packages dirs, and block the domain/IP at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for child process spawns from the installed package, .pth writes into site-packages, and outbound C2 from python; check whether PIP_INDEX_URL/PIP_CONFIG_FILE was set persistently to make the redirect survive.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe") or (FileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","python3","python") and ProcessCommandLine has "pip"))
| where ProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--index-url","--extra-index-url","--find-links")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\pip.exe","\\pip3.exe","\\python.exe","\\python3.exe")
| where CommandLine has "install"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--index-url","--extra-index-url","--find-links")
| where not(CommandLine has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Pip Install From Non-PyPI Index or Find-Links Source
id: 6b2f9c1a-8d4e-4a7b-9f21-3c7e5a1d0f42
description: Detects pip installing packages from an alternate index URL or find-links location that is not the official PyPI, matching the custom-repository hosting abuse described by Cisco Talos.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
  selection_flags:
    CommandLine|contains: 'install'
  selection_index:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--index-url'
      - '--extra-index-url'
      - '--find-links'
  filter_official:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'pypi.org'
      - 'files.pythonhosted.org'
  condition: selection_img and selection_flags and selection_index and not filter_official
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\pip.exe OR *\pip3.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\Python.exe) @CommandLine:*install* (@CommandLine:*--index-url* OR @CommandLine:*--extra-index-url* OR @CommandLine:*--find-links*) -(@CommandLine:*pypi.org* OR @CommandLine:*files.pythonhosted.org*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/(pip3?|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| CommandLine=/\binstall\b/i
| CommandLine=/--(index-url|extra-index-url|find-links)/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/(pypi\.org|files\.pythonhosted\.org)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `security_content_summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe") OR Processes.process="*-m pip*") Processes.process="*install*" (Processes.process="*--index-url*" OR Processes.process="*--extra-index-url*" OR Processes.process="*--find-links*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search NOT (process="*pypi.org*" OR process="*files.pythonhosted.org*") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false `security_content_summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe") OR Processes.process="*-m pip*") Processes.process="*install*" (Processes.process="*--index-url*" OR Processes.process="*--extra-index-url*" OR Processes.process="*--find-links*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search NOT (process="*pypi.org*" OR process="*files.pythonhosted.org*") | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Python setup.py install-time code execution spawning shell/LOLBin AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the article's core sdist build-hook abuse: setup.py executes arbitrary code the moment pip builds/installs a source distribution. Fires when a Python process running setup.py (or its pip parent) spawns a shell, script host, or download LOLBin. Rationale: Uses the article's central claim that setup.py 'executes automatically during installation, allowing for the execution of arbitrary code' — pivoting on the setup.py parent command line spawning a shell/download LOLBin. Falcon variant approximates via python/pip parent because FDR ProcessRollup2 does not expose parent command line. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/durabletask-teampcp-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit packages with C/C++ extensions whose setup.py shells out to a compiler wrapper or configure script during build
  • setup.py calling git.exe/curl to fetch version metadata or submodules at build time
  • Developer running 'python setup.py test' that invokes a shell-based test harness
  • Vendored build scripts that call certutil/bitsadmin for legitimate artifact retrieval on locked-down build agents
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cl.exe","gcc","clang","cmake","configure","vcvars"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child command line and the package name/path from InitiatingProcessCommandLine; decode any base64/encoded payload and identify the package being installed. 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and quarantine the sdist tarball + pip cache; pull the package from the resolved index and preserve setup.py. 3) Hunt: check other hosts that installed the same package name/version, look for .pth persistence written into site-packages, credential-file reads, and outbound connections from the python process during the install window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "setup.py"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash","sh","bash.exe","sh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "setup.py"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","bash","sh")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious .pth file dropped into site-packages by pip/python AIInstallation Medium
Hunts install-time persistence via a .pth file written into site-packages/dist-packages. Python auto-executes any line in a .pth file beginning with 'import' on every interpreter start, giving transient-to-persistent code execution — the TeamPCP litellm_init.pth technique that aligns with the article's persistent build-hook abuse. Rationale: Grounded in the article's 'Persistent' build-hook abuse row (setup.py+pyproject.toml, sdist+wheel) and corroborated by TeamPCP's litellm_init.pth in-package persistence; the site-packages/dist-packages path plus a .pth extension written by pip/python is the exact drop location, with the two standard tooling .pth files excluded. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/durabletask-teampcp-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teampcp-supply-chain-attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Editable installs (pip install -e .) dropping __editable__.<pkg>.pth or setuptools' generated .pth
  • Packages like matplotlib/pywin32/virtualenv legitimately shipping a .pth to extend sys.path
  • conda/virtualenv creation writing standard path-configuration .pth files
  • IDE (PyCharm/VS Code) creating a project .pth for interpreter path management
Suppression filter
| where not(FileName startswith "__editable__" or FileName in~ ("__editable___finder.pth","virtualenv.pth","pywin32.pth"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the .pth contents — a benign one contains only directory paths; flag any line starting with 'import' or containing exec/eval/base64. 2) Contain: if it executes code, isolate the host, delete/quarantine the .pth, and identify the parent package from the surrounding .dist-info. 3) Hunt: enumerate all interpreters on the host for the same .pth, sweep other endpoints that installed the same package/version, and correlate to any non-PyPI index redirect (UC1) or setup.py execution (UC2) in the same install window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".pth"
| where FolderPath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3")
| where not(FileName in~ ("easy-install.pth","distutils-precedence.pth"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".pth"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3")
| where not(TargetFileName in~ ("easy-install.pth","distutils-precedence.pth"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:*.pth (@TargetFilename:*site-packages* OR @TargetFilename:*dist-packages*) @Image:(*\pip.exe OR *\pip3.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\python3.exe OR *\Python.exe) -(@TargetFilename:*easy-install.pth OR @TargetFilename:*distutils-precedence.pth)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.pth$/i
| TargetFileName=/(site-packages|dist-packages)/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(pip3?|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| NOT (TargetFileName=/(easy-install|distutils-precedence)\.pth$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Persistent PIP_ index/config environment variable set in registry AIInstallation High
Alerts when a PIP_INDEX_URL / PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL / PIP_FIND_LINKS / PIP_CONFIG_FILE environment variable is written to the user or system Environment registry key. Per the article, any pip CLI arg converts to a PIP_<UPPER_LONG_NAME> env var — persisting one silently redirects ALL future pip installs to attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Directly operationalises the article's statement that any pip argument becomes a PIP_<UPPER_LONG_NAME> env var (naming PIP_CONFIG_FILE and PIP_FIND_LINKS) — writing these under the Environment registry key is a low-FP, high-fidelity redirect/persistence primitive. Falcon left empty: FDR does not reliably ship Session Manager\Environment writes as an AsepValueUpdate event. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/the-serpents-tongue-luring-the-python-out-of-its-den/ • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/defending_against_team_pcp_software_supply_chain_attacks/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1112 T1574.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer permanently pointing pip at a corporate mirror by setting PIP_INDEX_URL in user environment
  • IT provisioning script/GPO that pushes PIP_CONFIG_FILE to a managed pip.ini for all developers
  • CI runner bootstrap that exports PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL for a private feed
  • DevOps setting PIP_TARGET/PIP_PREFIX for a shared build environment
Suppression filter
| where not(RegistryValueData has_any ("artifactory","nexus","devpi","pkgs.dev.azure.com","codeartifact","jfrog.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read RegistryValueData — is the URL/config path an approved internal mirror or an external/unknown host? Identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and whether it was interactive or scripted. 2) Contain: if untrusted, delete the value, block the destination at the proxy, and audit any pip installs that ran after the value was set. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (non-PyPI index installs) and UC2/UC3 on the same host and any host sharing the GPO/provisioning source; verify no pip.ini/pip.conf on disk was also modified to the same destination.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Environment", @"Session Manager\Environment")
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("PIP_INDEX_URL","PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL","PIP_FIND_LINKS","PIP_CONFIG_FILE","PIP_TARGET","PIP_PREFIX")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Environment", @"Session Manager\Environment")
| where RegistryValue in~ ("PIP_INDEX_URL","PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL","PIP_FIND_LINKS","PIP_CONFIG_FILE","PIP_TARGET","PIP_PREFIX")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Miasma/AsyncAPI first-stage: node spawns detached 'node -e' downloader referencing IPFS/sync.js AIDelivery High
Hunts the AsyncAPI supply-chain first stage: a Node process spawns a detached child `node -e '<obfuscated>'` whose inline string table carries the plaintext IPFS gateway URL, the stage-2 CID, and the drop filename sync.js. Fires on package-import-triggered download rather than any npm lifecycle hook. Rationale: Anchored on verbatim strings from the shipped downloader string table (both IPFS CIDs, the ipfs.io gateway path, drop name sync.js) combined with the node->node -e detached-spawn shape. CIDs and the download-to-per-user-dir behaviour are confirmed by Wiz and SafeDep, so a require()-triggered node -e hit on these is unambiguous. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/miasma-malware-targets-npm-packages-and.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately scripting an IPFS pin/fetch with `node -e` against ipfs.io during dApp/Web3 work
  • CI job that inlines a node -e helper referencing a file literally named sync.js (rare)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox that is also EDR-monitored
  • Internal reproduction/IR testing of this exact payload after the advisory
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and confirm it contains an ipfs.io CID and sync.js; check the parent node process's working dir / project for an installed @asyncapi/specs@6.11.2(-alpha.1), @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, generator-helpers@1.1.1 or generator-components@0.7.1. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node child, and quarantine %LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS\sync.js (or ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound to 85.137.53.71 and for ~/.config/.miasma/ artifacts and miasma-monitor persistence; rotate any npm/GitHub/AWS tokens and SSH keys exposed on that host.

| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-e"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ipfs.io/ipfs/","Qmet4fhsAaWMBUxNDfREHwgiyDeSWy4YSYs9wiKUW5jGyf","QmQobZSp1wRPrpSEQ56qnyq7ecZh5Bg5k1fnjt4SUwwHb9","sync.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

Miasma stage-2 dropped: sync.js written to per-user NodeJS data directory AIInstallation High
Detects the second-stage loader landing on disk. The downloader writes the encrypted IPFS object as sync.js into the per-user Node data dir (%LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS on macOS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS on Linux), written by a node process. Rationale: The drop filename (sync.js) and the exact per-user NodeJS data directories are stated verbatim in the article and corroborated by SafeDep/Wiz as the stage-2 write location. A node-written sync.js in that dir has effectively no benign meaning — Node itself never creates that file there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unrelated Node tooling that coincidentally creates a cache file named sync.js under an app dir containing the token 'NodeJS' (uncommon)
  • EDR replay/rehydration of a quarantined sample regenerating the file
  • IR/forensic copy of the artifact onto a monitored analyst workstation
  • Backup/sync agent restoring an infected user profile
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped sync.js and compare against known stage-2 loaders (~8.24-8.25 MB); confirm the writing process is node and identify the parent project with an affected @asyncapi package. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, kill any node process executing it, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for outbound to 85.137.53.71, for ~/.config/.miasma/ identity/lock files and miasma-monitor persistence, and enumerate other hosts that installed the same @asyncapi versions in the compromise window.

| order by Timestamp desc

Miasma stage-2 executed: node runs sync.js from NodeJS data directory AIInstallation High
Detects execution of the dropped loader — a node process launched with a command line pointing at sync.js inside the per-user NodeJS data directory. This is the detached persistence/loader run that decrypts and evaluates the M-RED-TEAM stage-3 implant. Rationale: Distinct pivot from the first stage: instead of an inline node -e, this catches node executing the on-disk sync.js by path (NodeJS dir + sync.js), the stage-2 loader run. Path and filename are article-verbatim and corroborated as the loader location. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/
